claim: Hsp104 from Chaetomium thermophilum exhibits similar ATPase and protein remodeling activities to those of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae ortholog.
source: The Hsp104 disaggregase from Chaetomium thermophilum (CtHsp104), which exhibits similar ATPase and protein remodeling activities to those of the well-characterized Saccharomyces cerevisiae ortholog (ScHsp104) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A comparing activities of CtHsp104 and ScHsp104

claim: The crystal structure of the double Walker-B mutant of CtHsp104 in complex with ADP was determined at 3.7 Å resolution.
source: The crystal structure of the double Walker-B mutant in complex with ADP was determined at 3.7 Å resolution (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data collection and refinement statistics presented in Table 1

claim: The NTD was not defined by electron density in the crystal structure, likely due to high flexibility.
source: Although the obtained crystals are formed by the full-length protein (data not shown), the NTD was not defined by electron density, likely due to high flexibility.
evidence: Based on inference from crystallographic data and comparison with previous EM studies

claim: En-bloc mobility of the NTD has been reported in previous EM studies of related HSP100 enzymes.
source: Such en-bloc mobility was also reported in previous EM studies of related HSP100 enzymes (Ishikawa et al., 2004; Effantin et al., 2010; Carroni et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2003, 2007) and seems to be an inherent property of the domain, which is connected to the rest of the molecule by a long linker.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous EM studies

claim: The AAA1 and AAA2 domains consist of a large RecA-like α/β subdomain and a small α-helical ATPase subdomain.
source: The AAA1 and AAA2 domains consist of a large (L) RecA-like α/β and a small (S) α-helical ATPase subdomain.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: The large subdomains AAA1L and AAA2L are organized around a five-stranded parallel β-sheet that is flanked by three to four helices on either side.
source: Like in the crystal structure of the closely related ClpB disaggregase (Lee et al., 2003) that operates by the same basic mechanism as Hsp104 (Kummer et al., 2016), the large subdomains AAA1L and AAA2L are organized around a five-stranded parallel β-sheet that is flanked by three to four helices on either side.
evidence: Supported by structural data and comparison with ClpB structure

claim: The small C-terminal subdomains AAA1S and AAA2S have a four-helix bundle at their core, with one helix replaced by a three-stranded β-sheet in AAA2S.
source: The small C-terminal subdomains AAA1S and AAA2S have a four-helix bundle at their core, with one helix replaced by a three-stranded β-sheet in AAA2S.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: ADP molecules were clearly visible in the electron density map at the active sites.
source: The active sites, located at the AAA subdomain interface, are defined by co-crystallized ADP molecules, which were clearly visible in the electron density map (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by electron density map shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: In AAA1, ADP is accommodated in a pocket formed by Walker A, Walker B, sensor-1, and sensor-2 motifs.
source: In AAA1, ADP is accommodated in a pocket formed by the general Walker A (Lys229, Thr230) and Walker B (Asp295, Glu296) motifs as well as by AAA-specific (sensor-1: Thr330, sensor-2: Arg402) functional groups (Hanson and Whiteheart, 2005; Mogk et al., 2003; Hattendorf and Lindquist, 2002b).
evidence: Supported by structural data and citations to previous functional studies

claim: Arg349* protrudes into the active site and interacts with the Pα and Pβ of the bound ADP.
source: From here, Arg349* protrudes into the active site and interacts with the Pα and Pβ of the bound ADP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Arg349* has been previously described as the arginine finger critical for ATP binding and hydrolysis, and inter-subunit communication.
source: Consistent with its position close to the nucleotide phosphates, Arg349* has been previously described as the arginine finger critical for ATP binding and hydrolysis, and inter-subunit communication (Mogk et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous functional study

claim: AAA1 is distinguished from AAA2 by exhibiting a lower overall flexibility.
source: In addition to exhibiting a lower overall flexibility, AAA1 is distinguished from AAA2 by a prominent additional structure, the MD, which is an extension of AAA1S.
evidence: Based on structural observations from the crystal structure

claim: The MD motif comprises an elongated helix that pairs with its flanking helices via Leu-zipper interactions.
source: The MD motif comprises an elongated helix that pairs with its flanking helices via Leu-zipper interactions.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: The C-terminal blade (motif-2) of the MD binds to the AAA1 body via numerous polar contacts.
source: The C-terminal blade (motif-2) of the resultant propeller-like structure binds to the AAA1 body via numerous polar contacts, while the N-terminal blade (motif-1) protrudes away from the subunit to interact with a neighboring Hsp104 protomer.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: The N-terminal blade (motif-1) of the MD protrudes away from the subunit to interact with a neighboring Hsp104 protomer.
source: The C-terminal blade (motif-2) of the resultant propeller-like structure binds to the AAA1 body via numerous polar contacts, while the N-terminal blade (motif-1) protrudes away from the subunit to interact with a neighboring Hsp104 protomer.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: In the crystal, CtHsp104 subunits are arranged in a helical 61 filament.
source: In the crystal, CtHsp104 subunits are arranged in a helical 61 filament (Figure 1B) rather than forming a defined hexameric particle as observed in the recent cryo-electron microscopy structure of ScHsp104 (Yokom et al., 2016) or the crystal structure of a related HSP100 unfoldase, ClpC (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data and comparison with other structures

claim: The ClpC hexamer is planar.
source: It is interesting to note that while the ClpC hexamer is planar, the ScHsp104 hexamer shows a helical, staircase-like arrangement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with a smaller pitch but the same handedness as our crystallized filament.
evidence: Supported by comparison with ClpC crystal structure

claim: The ScHsp104 hexamer shows a helical, staircase-like arrangement with a smaller pitch but the same handedness as the crystallized CtHsp104 filament.
source: It is interesting to note that while the ClpC hexamer is planar, the ScHsp104 hexamer shows a helical, staircase-like arrangement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with a smaller pitch but the same handedness as our crystallized filament.
evidence: Supported by comparison with ScHsp104 cryo-EM structure

claim: CtHsp104 crystallization might have built upon an intrinsic tendency of Hsp104, and perhaps all HSP100 proteins, to switch between planar and helical conformations.
source: This suggests that CtHsp104 crystallization might have built upon an intrinsic tendency of Hsp104, and perhaps all HSP100 proteins, to switch between planar and helical conformations.
evidence: Based on inference from structural comparisons

claim: The architecture of the basic building blocks of AAA unfoldases, the rigid bodies, is comparable between the crystallized CtHsp104 filament and both ClpC and ScHsp104 hexameric structures.
source: Importantly, however, the crystallized filament seems to reflect mechanistic properties of the HSP100 hexamer, as the architecture of the basic building blocks of AAA unfoldases, the so-called rigid bodies, is comparable to that in both ClpC and ScHsp104 hexameric structures.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2

claim: The AAA rigid body comprises a mixed L/S* module formed between adjacent subunits.
source: As seen in previous crystal structures of hexameric unfoldases, the AAA rigid body comprises a mixed L/S* module formed between adjacent subunits (Glynn et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by structural data and citations to previous studies

claim: The AAA1L/AAA1S* and AAA2L/AAA2S* rigid bodies of the Hsp104 filament are very similar to those of the hexameric ScHsp104 and ClpC.
source: In fact, structural comparison shows that the AAA1L/AAA1S* and AAA2L/AAA2S* rigid bodies of the Hsp104 filament are very similar to those of the hexameric ScHsp104 and ClpC (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The sensor-2* helix accounts for about 75% of the inter-subunit interface (750 Å2 in total).
source: A central component tethering the L and S* subdomains is the sensor-2* helix, the helix following the sensor-2 residue (Hanson and Whiteheart, 2005), that accounts for about 75% of the inter-subunit interface (750 Å2 in total).
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: The properly arranged sensor-2* and SRH residues can perform their nucleotide-sensing task and coordinate the interplay of ATPase rigid bodies.
source: In concert, the properly arranged sensor-2* and SRH residues can perform their nucleotide-sensing task and coordinate the interplay of ATPase rigid bodies (Glynn et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by structural data and citations to previous functional studies

claim: In helical crystal structures of the bacterial homologue ClpB, the functional L/S* rigid bodies are not revealed.
source: It is important to note that, in contrast to the L/S* organization of Hsp104, helical crystal structures of the bacterial homologue ClpB (Carroni et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2003) do not reveal the functional L/S* rigid bodies (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison with ClpB structures

claim: In ClpB helical structures, the sensor-2 helix does not pair with the neighboring subunit and the composite sensor-2*/SRH motif is disrupted.
source: Here, the sensor-2 helix does not pair with the neighboring subunit and, consequently, the composite sensor-2*/SRH motif is disrupted.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison with ClpB structures

claim: In ClpB helical structures, the two subdomains are connected by a markedly reduced interface of 100–400 Å2, which is too small to support en-bloc movement of L and S*.
source: Moreover, the two subdomains are connected by a markedly reduced interface of 100–400 Å2, which is too small to support en-bloc movement of L and S*.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison with ClpB structures

claim: Residues mediating the Hsp104 L/S* contacts are highly conserved.
source: This notion is further corroborated by the observation that residues mediating the Hsp104 L/S* contacts are highly conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and match the hydrogen-exchange data of the related ClpB disaggregase (Oguchi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by sequence conservation analysis and comparison with hydrogen-exchange data

claim: Residues mediating the Hsp104 L/S* contacts match the hydrogen-exchange data of the related ClpB disaggregase.
source: This notion is further corroborated by the observation that residues mediating the Hsp104 L/S* contacts are highly conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and match the hydrogen-exchange data of the related ClpB disaggregase (Oguchi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparison with hydrogen-exchange data from ClpB

claim: The MD is critical for AAA1-AAA2 communication, Hsp70 binding, and keeping the enzyme inactive in the absence of cognate substrates.
source: Recent studies highlight the central role of the MD in regulating HSP100 disaggregases, as the domain is critical for AAA1-AAA2 communication, Hsp70 binding, and keeping the enzyme inactive in the absence of cognate substrates (Cashikar et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2013; Oguchi et al., 2012; Seyffer et al., 2012; Haslberger et al., 2007; Sielaff and Tsai, 2010; Miot et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The MD assembles a coiled-coil propeller that consists of motif-1 (residues 426–471) and motif-2 (residues 472–556).
source: As described, the MD assembles a coiled-coil propeller that consists of motif-1 (residues 426–471) and motif-2 (residues 472–556).
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: Adjacent MD propellers can interact in a head-to-tail fashion, whereby the tip of motif-1 contacts that of motif-2*, yielding a ring-like scaffold encircling the six AAA1 domains.
source: The adjacent propellers can interact in a head-to-tail fashion, whereby the tip of motif-1 contacts that of motif-2*, yielding a ring-like scaffold encircling the six AAA1 domains (Carroni et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by structural data and citation to previous study

claim: Binding of Hsp70 to the tip of motif-2 turns Hsp104 activity on, presumably by abrogating the MD-MD* interaction.
source: Binding of Hsp70 to the tip of motif-2 turns Hsp104 activity on, presumably by abrogating the MD-MD* interaction.
evidence: Based on inference from structural and functional data

claim: Site-specific mutations influencing the MD contacts can either disrupt the coiled-coil contacts, yielding a toxic, hyperactive Hsp104 variant that is constitutively 'on'.
source: Of note, site-specific mutations influencing the MD contacts have a similar regulatory effect (Supplementary file 1). They can either disrupt the coiled-coil contacts, yielding a toxic, hyperactive Hsp104 variant that is constitutively 'on' (Lee et al., 2005; Lipińska et al., 2013; Schirmer et al., 2004; Oguchi et al., 2012) or stabilize the MD-MD* interaction, yielding a repressed form that is strongly inhibited (Carroni et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous mutational studies

claim: Site-specific mutations influencing the MD contacts can stabilize the MD-MD* interaction, yielding a repressed form that is strongly inhibited.
source: Of note, site-specific mutations influencing the MD contacts have a similar regulatory effect (Supplementary file 1). They can either disrupt the coiled-coil contacts, yielding a toxic, hyperactive Hsp104 variant that is constitutively 'on' (Lee et al., 2005; Lipińska et al., 2013; Schirmer et al., 2004; Oguchi et al., 2012) or stabilize the MD-MD* interaction, yielding a repressed form that is strongly inhibited (Carroni et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous mutational studies

claim: Three main interfaces can be distinguished for intramolecular contacts between the MD and the ATPase core.
source: In particular, intramolecular contacts between the MD and the ATPase core are for the first time delineated with high precision. Accordingly, three main interfaces can be distinguished (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A

claim: An extensive network of polar interactions connects the central portion of the MD propeller to the AAA1 small subdomain of one ATPase module.
source: First, an extensive network of polar interactions connects the central portion of the MD propeller to the AAA1 small subdomain of one ATPase module.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: The MD binds to the neighboring ATPase module by docking the tip of motif-2, particularly Arg509, into a two-helix cleft on the edge of the AAA1 large subdomain.
source: In parallel, the MD binds to the neighboring ATPase module by docking the tip of motif-2, particularly Arg509, into a two-helix cleft on the edge of the AAA1 large subdomain.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: Several van-der-Waals contacts and hydrogen bonds connect the tips of motif-1 and motif-2* of two adjacent coiled-coils, yielding a continuous MD ring that wraps around the AAA1 core.
source: Finally, several van-der-Waals contacts and hydrogen bonds connect the tips of motif-1 and motif-2* of two adjacent coiled-coils, yielding a continuous MD ring that wraps around the AAA1 core.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: Every residue in the list of hyperactive mutations overlaps with one of the specific MD-AAA1 or MD-MD* contacts observed in the crystal structure.
source: The functional relevance of this interaction network is underscored by the fact that every residue in the list of hyperactive mutations overlaps with one of the specific MD-AAA1 or MD-MD* contacts observed in the crystal structure (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by structural data and comparison with known hyperactive mutations

claim: The predicted hyperactive mutants D247A and A446V displayed an elevated basal ATPase activity.
source: Most importantly, however, the predicted hyperactive mutants displayed an elevated basal ATPase activity, confirming that the contacts seen in the crystal structure are critical to regulate Hsp104.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: For AAA unfoldases to work, the ATPase modules need to move against each other in order to mechanically unfold client proteins.
source: In this regard, it should be noted that for AAA unfoldases to work, the ATPase modules need to move against each other in order to mechanically unfold client proteins (Olivares et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: In the proteasome, the ATP-driven conformational changes comprise pronounced en-bloc movements of the L/S* modules of about 15 Å.
source: As seen in the proteasome, the ATP-driven conformational changes comprise pronounced en-bloc movements of the L/S* modules of about 15 Å (Śledź et al., 2013), which would be hindered by an enclosing structural scaffold.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on the proteasome

claim: Superposition of the proteasomal ATPase core subunits Rpt1-6 on the modeled Hsp104 hexamer suggests that the MD scaffold may sterically impede conformational rearrangements of the ATPase rigid bodies.
source: Superposition of the proteasomal ATPase core subunits Rpt1-6 on the modeled Hsp104 hexamer suggests that the MD scaffold may sterically impede conformational rearrangements of the ATPase rigid bodies (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on structural modeling and comparison with proteasome structures

claim: The MD has a potential to establish a topological belt, a 'restraint mask', limiting movement and activity of the entrapped AAA1 domains.
source: Accordingly, the MD has a potential to establish a topological belt, a 'restraint mask', limiting movement and activity of the entrapped AAA1 domains.
evidence: Based on inference from structural data and modeling

claim: The number of distinct Lys-Lys cross-links determined in a comparative XL-MS analysis is useful to estimate protein dynamics in a semi-quantitative manner.
source: As reported recently, the number of distinct Lys-Lys cross-links determined in a comparative XL-MS analysis is useful to estimate protein dynamics in a semi-quantitative manner (Scorsato et al., 2016; Walzthoeni et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The most drastic variation in cross-linking was seen within the AAA1 ring, with four distinct cross-linked Lys-pairs in the repressive, eight in the wild-type, and 17 in the hyperactive Hsp104.
source: The most drastic variation was seen within the AAA1 ring, for which we identified four distinct cross-linked Lys-pairs in the repressive, eight in the wild-type, and 17 in the hyperactive Hsp104.
evidence: Supported by XL-MS experimental data

claim: The comparative XL-MS analysis supports the restraint-mask model, which predicts that a closed MD belt immobilizes the entrapped AAA1 ATPase modules, thereby keeping the Hsp104 disaggregase in its resting state.
source: In conclusion, the comparative XL-MS analysis supports the restraint-mask model, which predicts that a closed MD belt immobilizes the entrapped AAA1 ATPase modules, thereby keeping the Hsp104 disaggregase in its resting state.
evidence: Supported by XL-MS experimental data and inference

claim: Once the MD contacts are broken, the ATPase modules are free to move against each other to remodel engaged client proteins.
source: Once the MD contacts are broken, the ATPase modules are free to move against each other, as seen for the hyperactive mutant, to remodel engaged client proteins.
evidence: Based on inference from XL-MS data

claim: The G380C-Q491C mutant allows to covalently link motif-2 of the MD to the AAA1S subdomain thereby tethering neighboring ATPase bodies.
source: Using this G380C-Q491C mutant, it was possible to covalently link motif-2 of the MD to the AAA1S subdomain thereby tethering neighboring ATPase bodies.
evidence: Supported by experimental design and data

claim: Cys-Cys cross-linking yielded a fastened MD belt that almost completely abolished activity.
source: GFP unfolding and luciferase disaggregation assays revealed that the S-S bond formation upon Cys-Cys cross-linking yielded a fastened MD belt that almost completely abolished activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Introducing the 8-Å-long BMOE cross-linker at the same position restores flexibility of the MD and supports high unfolding and disaggregation capability.
source: In strong contrast, introducing the 8-Å-long BMOE cross-linker at the same position restores flexibility of the MD and supports high unfolding and disaggregation capability (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The cross-linking data support the restrain-mask model showing that AAA1 domains engaged by a covalently-linked but loosened MD belt can still reorient and cooperate with each other.
source: In conclusion, the cross-linking data support the restrain-mask model showing that AAA1 domains engaged by a covalently-linked but loosened MD belt can still reorient and cooperate with each other.
evidence: Based on inference from cross-linking experimental data

claim: Motif-2 binds via a conserved arginine to the same two-helix cleft in AAA1L in both Hsp104 and ClpB crystal structures.
source: As shown in the superposition (Hsp104 MD in yellow; ClpB MD conformations in red) and the zoomed-in windows, motif-2 binds via a conserved arginine to the same two-helix cleft in AAA1L.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5B

claim: The respective arginine residue (Arg509) has been identified in Hsp104 as an important functional group giving rise to hyperactive mutations.
source: Notably, the respective arginine residue (Arg509) has been identified in Hsp104 as an important functional group giving rise to hyperactive mutations (Biter et al., 2012a; Wendler et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous mutational studies

claim: By simultaneously binding to two AAA1 rigid bodies, motif-2 is capable of reducing the mobility and thus the activity of engaged ATPase modules.
source: The cross-linking data also delineate the key feature of the MD safety belt: By simultaneously binding to two AAA1 rigid bodies, motif-2 is capable of reducing the mobility and thus the activity of engaged ATPase modules.
evidence: Based on inference from cross-linking data and structural analysis

claim: In the crystal structure of Hsp104, the PS1-hairpin protrudes from the AAA2 into the AAA1* ring, where it is accommodated in a deep pocket close to the ATP binding site of a neighboring subunit.
source: Strikingly, in the crystal structure of Hsp104, the PS1-hairpin protrudes from the AAA2 into the AAA1* ring, where it is accommodated in a deep pocket close to the ATP binding site of a neighboring subunit (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The superposed rigid bodies of the ScHsp104 filament, including the PS1 motif, fit remarkably well to the rigid bodies of the planar and helical hexamers.
source: Except a few steric clashes with the flexible MD (clashes that could be avoided by a minor reorientation of the coiled-coil domain), the superposed rigid bodies of the ScHsp104 filament, including the PS1 motif, fit remarkably well to the rigid bodies of the planar and helical hexamers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural alignment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The PS1 motif is well positioned to functionally link the AAA1 and AAA2 rings in the various HSP100 oligomers.
source: These structural alignments suggest that the PS1 motif is well positioned to functionally link the AAA1 and AAA2 rings in the various HSP100 oligomers.
evidence: Based on inference from structural alignments

claim: Deleting the PS1-hairpin had only a minor effect on the overall ATPase activity.
source: Upon deleting the PS1-hairpin, we could measure only a minor effect on the overall ATPase activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The PS1 deletion fully blocked the unfoldase and disaggregase activities.
source: Despite leaving the ATPase engines largely untouched, the PS1 deletion, however, fully blocked the unfoldase and disaggregase activities (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Deleting the PS1 hairpin in the yeast Hsp104 had a similar effect, suggesting that the uncovered coupling is generally relevant for HSP100 disaggregases.
source: Notably, deleting the PS1 hairpin in the yeast Hsp104 had a similar effect, suggesting that the uncovered coupling is generally relevant for HSP100 disaggregases (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: The G731R mutant had a slightly decreased ATPase activity, but it was even more impaired in its unfoldase and disaggregase activity, thus mimicking the PS1 deletion phenotype.
source: When tested in our activity assays, the G731R mutant had a slightly decreased ATPase activity, but it was even more impaired in its unfoldase and disaggregase activity, thus mimicking the PS1 deletion phenotype (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: A reported mutation in the arginine residue at the tip of the PS1-hairpin in ClpB from Arabidopsis thaliana (R705K) led to a loss-of-function phenotype.
source: The in vivo relevance of the described PS1 interactions is also emphasized by a reported mutation in the arginine residue at the tip of the PS1-hairpin in ClpB from Arabidopsis thaliana that, despite its conservative character (R705K), led to a loss-of-function phenotype (Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Under conditions where ATP is stably bound to AAA1 (WB mutation), the AAA2 ring remains fully active.
source: Under the conditions where ATP is stably bound to AAA1 (WB mutation), the AAA2 ring remains fully active.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Preventing ATP binding to the AAA1 ring (WA mutation) turns AAA2 activity off.
source: In contrast, preventing ATP binding to the AAA1 ring (WA mutation) turns AAA2 activity off.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Deleting the PS1-hairpin abolishes the correlation between AAA1 and AAA2 and renders the AAA2 ring active independent of the nucleotide-binding state of AAA1.
source: Strikingly, deleting the PS1-hairpin abolishes this correlation and renders the AAA2 ring active independent of the nucleotide-binding state of AAA1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: The PS1-hairpin is critical for adjusting the nucleotide-binding properties of AAA1 and AAA2.
source: Moreover, the PS1-hairpin is critical for adjusting the nucleotide-binding properties of AAA1 and AAA2, which is particularly evident from the analysis of ATP binding to AAA2 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Using the AAA1 WA mutant, the observed affinity of AAA2 for ATP was very high (Kd≈0.1 μM), most likely due to an allosteric effect of an empty AAA1 on AAA2.
source: Using the AAA1 WA mutant, the observed affinity of AAA2 for ATP was very high (Kd≈0.1 μM), most likely due to an allosteric effect of an empty AAA1 on AAA2, as previously proposed (Franzmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to previous study

claim: Removal of the PS1-hairpin decreases the affinity of AAA2 for ATP by more than two orders of magnitude under conditions where AAA1 is in the apo state.
source: Removal of the PS1-hairpin decreases the affinity under these conditions by more than two orders of magnitude, suggesting that the allosteric control of AAA2 by AAA1 has now been compromised.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: The PS1 motif is the structural element coordinating the two ATPase engines of Hsp104.
source: Taken together, our structural and biochemical data demonstrate that the PS1 motif is the structural element coordinating the two ATPase engines of Hsp104.
evidence: Based on integration of structural and biochemical data

claim: The PS1-hairpin is directly connected via strand β4 with the sensor-1 motif of AAA2 (Asn748) that is critical for ATP hydrolysis.
source: First, the PS1-hairpin is directly connected via strand β4 with the sensor-1 motif of AAA2 (Asn748) that is critical for ATP hydrolysis (Hattendorf and Lindquist, 2002b).
evidence: Supported by structural data and citation to previous functional study

claim: The central β-sheet of AAA2 appears to be slightly distorted in the Hsp104 filament.
source: Secondly, the central β-sheet of AAA2 appears to be slightly distorted in the Hsp104 filament.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 7A

claim: In the Hsp104 oligomer, contacts to the AAA1 domain, as well as to neighboring AAA2 subunits, induce a distortion of the central β-sheet, in particular of the two capping strands.
source: Structural comparison with the isolated AAA2 domain from ClpB (Zeymer et al., 2014) suggests that in the Hsp104 oligomer, contacts to the AAA1 domain, as well as to neighboring AAA2 subunits, induce a distortion of the central β-sheet, in particular of the two capping strands (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison with isolated AAA2 domain

claim: Parallel β-sheets are presumed to be less stable than the anti-parallel counterparts and may thus be amenable to deformation.
source: Notably, parallel β-sheets are presumed to be less stable than the anti-parallel counterparts (Richardson, 1977) and may thus be amenable to such deformation.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on β-sheet stability

claim: The entrance point of the PS1-hairpin into the β-sheet of AAA2 is lined on one side by the strictly conserved Pro627, which does not form hydrogen bonds with the backbone of strand β4.
source: Furthermore, the entrance point of the PS1-hairpin into the β-sheet of AAA2 is lined on one side by the strictly conserved Pro627, which does not form hydrogen bonds with the backbone of strand β4.
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure

claim: The middle strand β4 may undergo small rearrangements within the frame of the central β-sheet, allowing the repositioning of the sensor-1 residue Asn748 (AAA2) via β4/PS1 in response to subunit reorientation in the AAA1 ring.
source: We hypothesize that, owing to the observed imperfect secondary structure, the middle strand β4 may undergo small rearrangements within the frame of the central β-sheet. Such mobility would allow the repositioning of the sensor-1 residue Asn748 (AAA2) via β4/PS1 in response to subunit reorientation in the AAA1 ring (Figure 7B).
evidence: Based on speculation from structural observations

claim: The PS1+ decoupling mutant (insertion of a single Gly residue between residues Asn740 and Cys741) led to a severe reduction in the unfolding and disaggregation activities, while the ATPase activity of AAA1 and AAA2 became partially uncoupled.
source: Similar to the ΔPS1 deletion, these mutations led to a severe reduction in the unfolding and disaggregation activities, while the ATPase activity of AAA1 and AAA2 became partially uncoupled (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2

claim: The PS1- mutant (shortening the PS1-hairpin by two residues, Δ737-738) led to a severe reduction in the unfolding and disaggregation activities, while the ATPase activity of AAA1 and AAA2 became partially uncoupled.
source: Similar to the ΔPS1 deletion, these mutations led to a severe reduction in the unfolding and disaggregation activities, while the ATPase activity of AAA1 and AAA2 became partially uncoupled (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2

claim: The PP mutant (modifying the central β-sheet of AAA2 by mutating the Pro-Pro-Ser motif of strand β1 by a less distorting sequence, P627T-P628G-S629N) led to a severe reduction in the unfolding and disaggregation activities, while the ATPase activity of AAA1 and AAA2 became partially uncoupled.
source: Similar to the ΔPS1 deletion, these mutations led to a severe reduction in the unfolding and disaggregation activities, while the ATPase activity of AAA1 and AAA2 became partially uncoupled (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
